subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 13 periods = 520 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

periods.textbook_anchor: Back to School from Holidays — Students fill a table recording places visited during holidays and note something special about each place, then compare their findings with friends (p. 131)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook picture of the four children — Chandni, Ritika, Gurpreet, Nayan — at the chapter opening

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites three or four students to share where they went during the holidays and one memorable thing about that place. Students listen and notice how different the places sound from one another.

Class opens Textbook p. 131 and reads the holiday stories of Chandni, Ritika, Gurpreet, and Nayan aloud together. Teacher points to the four different regions on a rough sketch drawn on the board — beach, desert, farm plains, mountains — and names each landform.

Each student fills the table on Textbook p. 131, recording the name of their own holiday place and something special about it, then asking two or three friends the same question and noting their answers. The class works quietly and independently.

Brief whole-class share-out: teacher asks, 'What similarities did you notice between your place and a friend's? What was very different?' Students share observations aloud. Teacher closes by naming the four landforms the chapter will explore.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record and compare features of different places by gathering information from peers and identifying similarities and differences.
periods.section_context: Holiday destinations shared by Chandni (Puri beach), Ritika (Rajasthan desert), Gurpreet (Amritsar plains), Nayan (Sikkim mountains); student-recorded holiday places and peer comparison table.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did anyone visit a place that felt completely unlike your own town — what felt most different?' Encourage students whose families did not travel to describe a place they have heard about or seen in pictures.

periods.section_ref: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet — Students look at the picture of everyday life in Punjab and write observations about the land, activities, animals, and clothing (p. 132)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook picture of Punjab plains — farmers, tractors, animals, traditional Punjabi clothing

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to look silently at the picture on Textbook p. 132 for a full minute without speaking, noticing as many details as they can.

Students write their observations in notebooks, answering the four questions from Textbook p. 132: what kind of land, what activities, which animals, and what is unique about the clothing. Teacher circulates, prompting students who finish early to count how many different activities they spotted.

Whole-class discussion: teacher draws four columns on the board (Land / Activities / Animals / Clothing) and students call out their observations to fill each column. Teacher adds any feature students missed and reads aloud the text about fertile soil, farming, makki di roti, sarson da saag, lassi, and the Golden Temple's langar sewa.

Students are invited to share whether any food or farming practice from the picture reminds them of something from their own region. Teacher names the connection between fertile flat land and the farming life as the first landform-culture link the chapter builds.

periods.implied_lo: Students can make structured written observations of a picture, organising what they see into categories such as land type, activities, animals, and clothing.
periods.section_context: Punjab plains picture; fertile soil; farming with tractors and animals; traditional Punjabi attire; makki di roti, sarson da saag, lassi; Golden Temple, langar sewa.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'How does the flat, fertile land make farming possible here — what would happen if the land were rocky or full of sand?' If students mention the Golden Temple's langar, draw out the idea of sharing food with everyone as a community tradition.

periods.activity_title: Our Region's Food — Ingredients and Stories
periods.section_ref: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet — Students name the most popular food in their own region and list its main ingredients (p. 133)
materials: Crayons or sketch pens (optional, for illustration)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Textbook p. 133 prompt aloud and asks students to think quietly: what is one food their family makes that feels special to their region? Students are encouraged to picture the dish — its colour, smell, what goes into it.

Each student writes the name of their regional food and lists its main ingredients in their notebook, following the format on Textbook p. 133. Students who wish may also draw a small picture of the dish beside their writing.

Students share in pairs: each partner reads their food and ingredients aloud, and together they notice one ingredient that appears in both dishes and one that is completely different. Two or three pairs share with the class.
Teacher draws together: 'Look at how the land affects what grows there, and how what grows shapes what people eat.' Students name the food-land connection as a short oral round-up.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe a regional food tradition by naming a dish and its key ingredients, and connect it to the natural environment of that region.
periods.section_context: Students' own regional food items and ingredients; Punjab foods — makki di roti, sarson da saag, lassi; farming plains as source of ingredients.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: This task naturally draws out regional and family variety — accept all answers as equally valid. Ask: 'Where does the main ingredient come from — is it grown locally?' to help students start connecting food to land.

periods.activity_title: Desert Picture Observation and Water Scarcity Discussion
periods.section_ref: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika — Students look at the desert village picture and write observations about land, plants, clothing, and travel (p. 135)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook picture of Rajasthan desert village — sand, cactus, people in colourful clothing, camel

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'Has anyone seen a desert — in real life, a film, or a book? What did it look like?' Students share briefly. Teacher then asks everyone to open Textbook p. 135 and observe the picture silently.

Students write their observations in notebooks, answering the five questions from Textbook p. 135: kind of land, types of plants and how they differ from local plants, unique dress, how people might travel, and what they like most in the picture.

Class reads together the text about desert plants (cactus, khejri, babool), animals (camel, lizard, eagle, python, wild cat), traditional clothing (ghaghras, bandhini dupattas, turbans), and tankas for water storage. Teacher notes the word 'tanka' on the board and asks students what problem it solves.

Brief oral discussion on Textbook p. 138: 'Why is water scarce in the desert?' Students offer reasons and teacher guides them to the idea of very little rainfall — the land itself shapes how people store and use water.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record features of a landscape — its plants, animals, clothing, and adaptations — by interpreting a picture and organising their findings in writing.
periods.section_context: Rajasthan desert picture; sand, cactus, khejri, babool; camel, lizard, wild cat, python, eagle; ghaghras, bandhini dupattas, turbans; tanka water storage; water scarcity discussion.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why do you think the plants in the desert look so different from plants near a river or pond?' Guide students to notice that the tanka is a local solution to a local problem — communities invented it without outside help.

periods.activity_title: Desert Culture — Folk Arts from Our Families
periods.section_ref: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika — Students ask family members about folk songs and dances from their own region and record them in a table (p. 137)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of Rajasthani folk musicians and dancers (khartal, sarangi)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the description of Rajasthani folk music instruments (khartal, sarangi) and colourful folk dances from the textbook text. Students listen and the teacher asks: 'Do any of you know a folk song or dance from your own home or community?'

Students open Textbook p. 137 and, using what they recall from conversations at home or their own experience, fill the table with folk songs and dances from their region — naming the song or dance, when it is performed, and who performs it. Students who are unsure are encouraged to write what they have heard a grandparent or neighbour mention.

Small groups of three share what they wrote. The class notices: are there folk forms that several students share? Are there any that are completely new to others? Two or three students share with the whole class.

Teacher connects: 'Just as Rajasthan has its khartal and sarangi, every region has its own musical tradition — these are gifts passed down through families.' The class names one or two traditions they found most interesting.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe folk music and dance traditions of their own and other regions by drawing on family knowledge and expressing it in a structured written form.
periods.section_context: Rajasthani folk instruments — khartal, sarangi; folk dances; student-recorded folk songs and dances from their own families and regions.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why do you think folk songs are different in different places — what do they sing about?' Affirm all regional answers as equally rich. If students mention harvest songs, wedding songs, or rain songs, note how these connect to the land and seasons.

periods.activity_title: Seashore Observations — Life by the Water
periods.textbook_anchor: On the Seashore, with Chandni — Students look at the seashore picture and write observations about activities, trees, beach activities, and coastal clothing (p. 139)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook picture of Puri seashore — fishing boats, coconut palms, people in coastal clothing

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to close their eyes and imagine standing at a beach — what do they hear, smell, and see? Students share a few images aloud, then open Textbook p. 139 to compare the picture with their imagination.

Students write their observations answering the four questions from Textbook p. 139: activities people are doing, trees found near the sea and how they differ from desert trees, fun activities they would like to do, and what is special about coastal dress.

Whole-class reading of the section on Puri: Shree Jagannath Temple, Rath Yatra, Odissi dance, Sambalpuri sarees, traditional foods (dalma, pakhala, chhena poda, rasagola), and the shankh used in religious rituals. Students identify the features that connect sea life to culture.
Students do the marine creature identification task from Textbook p. 142 — matching names to pictures of sea turtle, crab, dolphin, corals, seaweed, and starfish — and check answers with a partner.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and describe features of a coastal environment — its trees, animals, human activities, and cultural practices — by reading a picture and connecting it to textbook information.
periods.section_context: Puri seashore picture; coconut palms; fishing boats; Shree Jagannath Temple; Rath Yatra; Odissi dance; Sambalpuri sarees; dalma, pakhala, chhena poda, rasagola; shankh; sea turtle, crab, dolphin, corals, seaweed, starfish.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'How do the trees near the sea look different from the cactus in the desert — why might that be?' When shankh comes up, ask students whether they have seen conch shells at home or in temples, linking the coastal environment to everyday religious life.

periods.activity_title: Coastal Craft — Making a Decor Object
periods.textbook_anchor: On the Seashore, with Chandni — Students use one coastal item to create a decorative object such as a photo frame, necklace, painted pebble, mini basket, or sand art jar (p. 141)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of coastal craft examples (p. 141)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the activity description from Textbook p. 141 aloud and shows the available materials on the desk. Students discuss briefly in pairs which type of decor object they want to make and which material they will use as their 'coastal item'.

Students create their chosen coastal-inspired decor object — a painted pebble, a cardboard photo frame decorated with seeds and leaves, a string necklace, or their own invention. Teacher circulates, asking students to describe what their object represents about coastal life.

Students hold up or place their finished objects on the desk. A quick gallery walk: students move around to look at two or three nearby objects and compliment one feature they notice. Each creator names the coastal element they represented.

Teacher closes: 'Artists in coastal regions have been making beautiful objects from things the sea and shore provide — this is how craft and environment come together.' Students name one such tradition they encountered in the section.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express an understanding of a regional environment by creating and explaining a craft object that draws on the natural materials or cultural symbols of that region.
periods.section_context: Coastal-inspired decor craft — painted pebble, photo frame, necklace, mini basket, sand art jar; coastal materials (pebbles, seeds, leaves); connection to coastal craft traditions of Odisha.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What does your object tell someone about life near the sea — if a friend from the mountains saw it, what would they learn?' Encourage creative choices and assure students that any object inspired by the coast is valid, whatever materials they used.

periods.activity_title: Cyclones, Clean Beaches, and Community Readiness
periods.textbook_anchor: On the Seashore, with Chandni — Students discuss the adverse effects of a cyclone and how communities can better prepare for such situations (p. 143)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image or description of cyclone damage in coastal Odisha

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students whether they have heard of a cyclone — from news, family stories, or their own experience. Students share what they know. Teacher reads aloud the textbook passage on cyclones, the damage they cause, and Odisha's award-winning disaster management practices.
Students discuss in small groups: 'What are the adverse effects of a cyclone?' Each group lists three or four effects in their notebooks. Groups share and a class list is built on the board.

Discussion continues with the second question from Textbook p. 143: 'How can communities be better prepared for such situations?' Students bring in ideas about early warnings, safe shelters, helping neighbours, and keeping evacuation routes clear. Teacher also draws out the beach-cleanliness discussion from Textbook p. 142 — why clean beaches matter for both safety and marine life.

Students write two or three sentences in their notebooks: one effect of a cyclone and one preparation step communities can take. Teacher closes by naming coastal communities' resilience as something built over generations.

periods.implied_lo: Students can discuss the impact of a natural hazard on a community and suggest preparation steps, drawing on both textbook information and their own reasoning.
periods.section_context: Cyclones; adverse effects of cyclones in coastal Odisha; Government of Odisha's disaster management; community preparedness; beach cleanliness and marine life.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you lived near a coast and heard a cyclone warning, what would be the first three things you would do?' Guide students toward thinking about people who cannot easily leave — elderly neighbours, fishing families who depend on their boats.

periods.activity_title: Mountain Picture Walk and Climate-Culture Links
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Mountains, with Nayan — Students look at the mountain picture and write observations about animals, dress, and trees (p. 145)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook picture of Sikkim mountains — yaks, people in traditional dress, oak and pine trees, snow-capped peaks

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to compare the temperature where they are today with how they imagine Gangtok in winter. Students guess and teacher confirms — cold, often snowy, steep slopes. Students open Textbook p. 145 and look at the picture.

Students write their observations answering the three questions from Textbook p. 145: what animals they see, how the mountain people's dress differs from their own region's dress, and how they would describe the trees in the picture.

Whole-class reading of the Sikkim section: yaks, mountain animals, oak, pine, walnut, chestnut trees; traditional dress (bakhu, dumdyam, Gunyo cholo); food (thukpa, sel roti); festivals (Loosong and Namsoong — Sikkimese New Year, chaam mask dance); traditional wooden houses with slanting roofs. Teacher asks students why slanting roofs make sense in a place with heavy rainfall and snow.

Discussion questions from Textbook p. 147 — how cold climate affects clothing and lifestyle, and why certain trees like pine and oak grow better in mountains — handled as a quick oral round. Students add any new detail to their notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe the features of a mountain environment — its animals, vegetation, and human adaptations in dress and housing — by reading a picture and connecting it to written information.
periods.section_context: Sikkim mountain picture; yaks; oak, pine, walnut, chestnut trees; bakhu, dumdyam, Gunyo cholo; thukpa, sel roti; Loosong and Namsoong festivals; chaam mask dance; wooden houses with slanting roofs; cold climate.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why do you think people in cold mountains wear thick, wrapped clothing rather than loose cotton — how does the body stay warm?' If students mention yaks, ask what makes the yak so useful in a cold, steep place compared to a horse or camel.

periods.activity_title: Landslides, Animal Adaptations, and Mountain Readiness
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Mountains, with Nayan — Students discuss why landslides are common in mountains during the rainy season and what can be done to keep people safe (p. 148)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image or description of landslide in a mountain region

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'Has anyone seen or heard about a landslide — on the news, or from family?' Students share. Teacher reads the relevant passage from Textbook p. 148 about why landslides happen in mountains during the rainy season.

Small groups discuss three questions from Textbook p. 148: why landslides happen in the rainy season; what can be done to keep people safe during landslides; and what communities can do to help those who lose their homes or are affected by natural disasters. Groups record key ideas.

Groups share their ideas. Teacher builds a class list of preparation and community support steps on the board. Teacher also takes the discussion questions from Textbook p. 147 on yak survival in the cold and house features (slanting roofs) — students share answers and teacher confirms with textbook content.

Students write three sentences in their notebooks: one reason landslides occur, one safety step, and one thing they notice about houses in their own locality that is similar to or different from Sikkimese slanting-roof houses.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain why a natural hazard occurs in a specific landform and identify safety and community response measures, using reasoning grounded in the features of that environment.
periods.section_context: Landslides in mountains during rainy season; yak adaptation to cold; slanting-roof wooden houses in Sikkim; community support for disaster-affected people; mountain region safety measures.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If someone's home is damaged by a landslide, who in the community can help, and how?' Guide students toward concrete, local actions — sharing food, shelter, helping rebuild — rather than abstract ideas. Connect to how Odisha's coastal communities prepare for cyclones (content built in the seashore section) as a parallel.

periods.activity_title: Drawing My Landform — People, Professions, and Place
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in my Landform — Students draw the landform of their own region and annotate it with the area name, landform type, people, professions, food, houses, plants, and animals (p. 149)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the task from Textbook p. 149 aloud. Students think quietly for a moment: what landform do they live in or near? Teacher asks a few students to name their landform type — plains, coast, hills, or another — so everyone has a starting point.

Students draw their local landform on a page and annotate it with labels: the name of the area, the landform type, the kind of people and their professions, local food, housing style, characteristic plants, and animals. Teacher circulates and asks individual students questions to prompt richer labels.
Students share their drawing with the person next to them. Partners identify one feature they share and one that is different. Two or three students hold up their drawings for the class to see.

Teacher closes: 'Every one of these drawings is a record of a real place and real lives — the landform shapes everything you drew.' Students are invited to keep the drawing as a personal reference for the chapter.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent their own geographical environment through annotated drawing, labelling the natural features and human practices that characterise it.
periods.section_context: Students' own local landform; landform type (plains, coast, hills, etc.); local people and professions; local food; housing style; characteristic plants and animals.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What is the one feature of your landform that most shapes how people live there — and why?' Accept all landform types and regional varieties; a student from a hilly town and one from a riverine plain are both correct.

periods.activity_title: Comparing Four Landforms — The Big Table
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in my Landform — Students fill a comparative table with columns for Plains, Desert, Coastal, and Mountains across rows of trees, animals, housing, clothing, food, festivals, and art forms (p. 150)
periods.visual_aids: Board table drawn by teacher — columns: Plains, Desert, Coastal, Mountains; rows: Trees, Animals, Housing, Clothing, Food, Festivals, Art forms

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the comparative table on the board with all four columns and seven rows. Students open Textbook p. 150 and look at the empty table. Together the class fills in one example row — 'Trees' — as a shared warm-up, recalling cactus and khejri for desert, coconut palms for coast, oak and pine for mountains, and wheat and mustard fields for plains.

Students work independently to fill the remaining rows in the table using what they have read and discussed throughout the chapter. Teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck by asking: 'What did Gurpreet eat? What did Nayan wear? What kind of house did Ritika describe?'
Class fills in the board table row by row, with students calling out their answers. Teacher confirms, corrects, and adds any missed detail. Students update their own tables.

Teacher asks: 'Looking at the whole table — which landform feels most like your own, and which feels most different?' Students answer orally. Teacher names the table as a record of how India's landforms have shaped four very different ways of life.

periods.implied_lo: Students can systematically compare features of different environments across multiple categories by completing a structured table that draws on details observed and discussed across a chapter.
periods.section_context: Comparative table — Plains (wheat, mustard, farming, makki di roti, langar), Desert (cactus, khejri, camel, mud houses with tanka, dal-bati-churma, ghaghras), Coastal (coconut palms, fishing, sea creatures, Rath Yatra, Odissi dance), Mountains (oak, pine, yak, slanting-roof wooden houses, thukpa, Loosong); categories: trees, animals, housing, clothing, food, festivals, art forms.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why does the same category — for example, housing — look so different across the four columns? What is the landform's role in that?' Guide students to see the table not as a list to memorise but as a pattern that shows land-culture connections.

periods.textbook_anchor: Life in my Landform — Students design and draw an imaginary landform combining favourite features from mountains, plains, coasts, and deserts, then discuss why they chose each feature and what difficulties people might face (p. 151)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the task from Textbook p. 151: 'You can now design your own imaginary landform — pick your favourite features from any of the four landforms. What would you most want to live near?' Students think silently and decide on two or three features they will combine.

Students draw their imaginary landform on a page. Alongside or beneath the drawing they write: what they chose from each landform, why they chose it (what benefit it brings to people, animals, or plants), and one difficulty people might face in their invented land.

Students share in pairs, walking each other through their drawing and the choices behind it. Three or four students share with the whole class, naming the most interesting benefit and the biggest challenge in their design. Class listens for surprising combinations.

Teacher closes the chapter: 'Every landform in India offers something precious — and every one also brings its own challenges. The people who live there have found ways to make it home.' Students are invited to name one thing from the chapter they will remember.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design and justify a creative synthesis by selecting features from different environments, explaining the benefits each feature provides and the challenges it poses.
periods.section_context: Imaginary landform combining features from mountains, plains, coasts, deserts; student-selected features and their benefits to people, animals, or plants; challenges people might face in the designed landform.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you chose a beach AND snowy mountains for your landform, how would people dress — and would that be easy?' Push students to reason through the consequences of their design choices, not just list what they like.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain why a natural hazard occurs in a specific landform and identify safety and community response measures, using reasoning grounded in the features of that environment.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Landslides in mountains during rainy season; yak adaptation to cold; slanting-roof wooden houses in Sikkim; community support for disaster-affected people; mountain region safety measures.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: In the Mountains, with Nayan — Students discuss why landslides are common in mountains during the rainy season and what can be done to keep people safe (p. 148)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students discuss landslide causes and safety measures in groups, share community support ideas, and write a personal response connecting mountain environment features to disaster risk and resilience.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can represent their own geographical environment through annotated drawing, labelling the natural features and human practices that characterise it.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Students' own local landform; landform type (plains, coast, hills, etc.); local people and professions; local food; housing style; characteristic plants and animals.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Life in my Landform — Students draw the landform of their own region and annotate it with the area name, landform type, people, professions, food, houses, plants, and animals (p. 149)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students draw and annotate their own local landform with labels for people, professions, food, housing, plants, and animals, then share with a partner and identify one shared and one different feature.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can systematically compare features of different environments across multiple categories by completing a structured table that draws on details observed and discussed across a chapter.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Comparative table — Plains (wheat, mustard, farming, makki di roti, langar), Desert (cactus, khejri, camel, mud houses with tanka, dal-bati-churma, ghaghras), Coastal (coconut palms, fishing, sea creatures, Rath Yatra, Odissi dance), Mountains (oak, pine, yak, slanting-roof wooden houses, thukpa, Loosong); categories: trees, animals, housing, clothing, food, festivals, art forms.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Life in my Landform — Students fill a comparative table with columns for Plains, Desert, Coastal, and Mountains across rows of trees, animals, housing, clothing, food, festivals, and art forms (p. 150)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students complete a four-column comparative table across seven categories of landform life, co-construct the answers as a class, and reflect on which landform feels most like and most different from their own.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can design and justify a creative synthesis by selecting features from different environments, explaining the benefits each feature provides and the challenges it poses.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Imaginary landform combining features from mountains, plains, coasts, deserts; student-selected features and their benefits to people, animals, or plants; challenges people might face in the designed landform.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Life in my Landform — Students design and draw an imaginary landform combining favourite features from mountains, plains, coasts, and deserts, then discuss why they chose each feature and what difficulties people might face (p. 151)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students design and draw an imaginary composite landform, write justifications for their choices, share with peers, and discuss how each feature benefits or challenges those who might live there.

assessment_items.question_text: Chandni visited a beach in Odisha, Ritika went to a desert in Rajasthan, Gurpreet was at the plains in Punjab, and Nayan stayed in the mountains of Sikkim. Which of the following correctly matches a child to the landform they visited?
assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item checks whether students accurately recall the four child-landform pairings established in the chapter's opening section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record and compare features of different places by gathering information from peers and identifying similarities and differences.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses Chandni's coastal destination with the mountains, perhaps mixing up two unfamiliar regions.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses Gurpreet's plains (Amritsar) with a coastal region, suggesting the child did not retain the four region pairings from the opening activity.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Swaps Nayan's mountain home with the plains, indicating the child may have merged the Punjab and Sikkim details.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at this description of a Punjab village: farmers use tractors and bullocks, fields are flat and green, people wear bright phulkari-embroidered clothes. Write two things you can observe about the land and two things you can observe about the people in this description.
expected_elements: One observation about the land — e.g., the land is flat, the fields are green or fertile, the land is used for farming.
A second observation about the land — e.g., tractors and bullocks work on it, suggesting it is open and accessible.
One observation about the people — e.g., they are farmers or engaged in agriculture.
A second observation about the people — e.g., they wear traditionally embroidered clothing.
assessment_items.annotation: Full marks for any two land observations and any two people observations that are clearly drawn from the description. Accept paraphrase and local equivalent expressions.
assessment_items.chapter_section: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can make structured written observations of a picture, organising what they see into categories such as land type, activities, animals, and clothing.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

expected_elements: One observation about the land — e.g., the land is flat, the fields are green or fertile, the land is used for farming.
A second observation about the land — e.g., tractors and bullocks work on it, suggesting it is open and accessible.
One observation about the people — e.g., they are farmers or engaged in agriculture.
A second observation about the people — e.g., they wear traditionally embroidered clothing.

assessment_items.task: Think of a popular food from your region. Write its name and list at least three ingredients used to make it. Then write one sentence explaining where the main ingredient comes from — does it grow in your region?
assessment_items.scaffold:
Name of food: ___
Ingredients: (1) ___ (2) ___ (3) ___
The main ingredient comes from: ___
format_of_output: List of at least three ingredients
One sentence connecting main ingredient to the local land or region
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any regional food and any ingredients the student knows. The land-connection sentence is the key evaluative element — it should show the student understands that food ingredients come from the environment around them. Regional variation is expected and correct: a student from a coastal area naming rice and fish, a student from the plains naming wheat, and a student from a hilly area naming buckwheat are all equally valid answers.
assessment_items.chapter_section: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe a regional food tradition by naming a dish and its key ingredients, and connect it to the natural environment of that region.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can name a real regional food with its ingredients and make an explicit connection between the land and what it produces.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The food name and ingredient list show recall and knowledge of local culture; the final sentence is the reasoning step that shows whether the student links environment to food.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: specific local food name, three or more real ingredients, clear sentence connecting main ingredient to what grows or is available locally. Weak: generic food name with no ingredients, or ingredients listed without any land-connection sentence.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot write may draw the dish and label the ingredients; the teacher scribes the land-connection sentence from what the student says aloud.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Written list with one explanatory sentence
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The scaffold separates the recall task (food and ingredients) from the reasoning task (land connection), making it manageable for Grade IV students and easy for the teacher to evaluate each element separately.

assessment_items.question_text: People in Rajasthan's desert built tankas in their homes. What problem does a tanka solve?

options.label: A
options.text: It collects and stores rainwater for use during dry periods.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a type of underground room for sleeping in summer.

options.label: C
options.text: It keeps animals cool during sandstorms.

options.label: D
options.text: It stores food grains during the hot season.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. The tanka is a traditional water tank that collects rainwater — a local solution to the desert's scarcity of fresh water.
assessment_items.chapter_section: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record features of a landscape — its plants, animals, clothing, and adaptations — by interpreting a picture and organising their findings in writing.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses the tanka with a grain store — the student may have remembered 'storage' from the section but not the specific content stored.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Invents a function not mentioned in the chapter — the student may be guessing based on the desert heat rather than reading the text.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses tanka with a stepwell or underground chamber — the student may be mixing up different traditional structures mentioned in broader discussion.

assessment_items.question_text: Rajasthan is famous for folk music played on the khartal and sarangi. Name one folk song or dance tradition from your own region and describe when or why it is performed.
expected_elements: Name of a folk song or dance from the student's own region.
Description of when it is performed — e.g., at a harvest, a wedding, a festival, a seasonal event.
Any detail about who performs it or what mood or purpose it carries.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any genuine folk tradition the student names from any region. Regional variation is expected and all answers are correct. The key evaluative element is the 'when or why' — the student should connect the tradition to a context, not merely name it.
assessment_items.chapter_section: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe folk music and dance traditions of their own and other regions by drawing on family knowledge and expressing it in a structured written form.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

expected_elements: Name of a folk song or dance from the student's own region.
Description of when it is performed — e.g., at a harvest, a wedding, a festival, a seasonal event.
Any detail about who performs it or what mood or purpose it carries.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes the coastal region of Puri, Odisha. Which of the following is a feature of coastal areas as described in the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Coconut trees do not grow near the sea because of salty air.

options.label: B
options.text: Fishing is a primary livelihood, and the sea is home to creatures like dolphins and sea turtles.

options.label: C
options.text: People store rainwater in tankas because the coast is very dry.

options.label: D
options.text: The main livelihood of people is farming wheat on flat plains.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. Fishing and marine biodiversity are core features of the coastal section. Options A and C draw on content from the plains and desert sections respectively.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and describe features of a coastal environment — its trees, animals, human activities, and cultural practices — by reading a picture and connecting it to textbook information.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses coastal livelihood with the plains farming section — the student may not have retained the landform-livelihood connections.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Applies the tanka detail from the desert section to the coast — the student may be mixing up two sections' water-related content.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Contradicts the textbook, which mentions coconut palms as characteristic coastal trees — the student may be guessing or misremembering.

assessment_items.task: Use materials available to you — a pebble, a piece of cardboard, string, dried leaves, seeds, or sketch pens — to create a small decor object inspired by life near the sea. When you finish, write two sentences below it: one explaining what coastal feature your object represents, and one explaining what material from the sea or shore you imagined using.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My object is: ___
It represents this coastal feature: ___
The coastal material I imagined using: ___
format_of_output: A small handmade decor object (painted pebble, decorated frame, string necklace, or similar)
Two written sentences explaining the coastal feature represented and the imagined coastal material
assessment_items.annotation: Evaluate the written explanation, not the craft quality. A strong response names a specific coastal feature (e.g., shells, sand, fishing nets, waves) and explains how the object connects to that feature. Accept any coastal reference from the Odisha coastal section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express an understanding of a regional environment by creating and explaining a craft object that draws on the natural materials or cultural symbols of that region.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can connect creative work to geographical knowledge — not just make an object but explain what it represents about coastal life.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The object itself shows engagement with the creative mode; the two sentences are the assessment element — they reveal whether the student can articulate the coastal connection.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: object clearly relates to coastal life, sentences name a specific coastal feature and a real material from the shore. Weak: generic object with no connection to coastal life, or sentences that describe what the object looks like rather than what it represents.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find making difficult may draw their object instead; students who struggle to write may dictate the two sentences to the teacher.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Craft object plus two written sentences
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The craft mode matches the C&E dominant mode of this period; the written sentences provide the teacher with an observable, assessable explanation of the student's understanding.

assessment_items.question_text: Imagine you live in a village on the coast of Odisha. The weather forecast says a cyclone is coming in two days. Write what steps you and your community should take to stay safe and help each other.
look_for: Mentions at least one step taken before the cyclone arrives — e.g., moving to a shelter, securing boats, storing food and water.
Mentions helping a neighbour, elderly person, or someone who cannot move on their own.
Shows understanding that cyclones cause damage to homes, crops, or the environment.
Suggests at least one community-level action — e.g., sharing supplies, listening to official warnings, working together to protect property.
Writing reflects awareness that people living near the coast face this hazard regularly and have developed responses to it.
assessment_items.annotation: This is an evaluative reasoning item. There is no single correct answer. Award marks for concrete, realistic steps that show the student understands both the hazard and the role of community. Deduct nothing for imperfect spelling or grammar.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can discuss the impact of a natural hazard on a community and suggest preparation steps, drawing on both textbook information and their own reasoning.

competency.competency_text: Discusses how to prepare for emergency situations (smoke, fire, small injuries, burns, electrical safety, unseasonal rains, fallen trees) based on discussions with family and community, or personal experiences

look_for: Mentions at least one step taken before the cyclone arrives — e.g., moving to a shelter, securing boats, storing food and water.
Mentions helping a neighbour, elderly person, or someone who cannot move on their own.
Shows understanding that cyclones cause damage to homes, crops, or the environment.
Suggests at least one community-level action — e.g., sharing supplies, listening to official warnings, working together to protect property.
Writing reflects awareness that people living near the coast face this hazard regularly and have developed responses to it.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes traditional houses in Sikkim as being built with wood and having slanting roofs. Give two reasons why this design makes sense for the mountain climate and environment.
expected_elements: One reason connected to heavy rainfall — e.g., slanting roofs allow rain or snow to slide off quickly, preventing the roof from collapsing under weight.

One reason connected to the cold climate or local resources — e.g., wood is available in mountain forests and is a good insulator against the cold; OR steep slopes mean flat-roofed structures would be harder to build and maintain.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two reasons that logically connect the house feature to the mountain environment. Reasoning does not have to match the textbook verbatim — a student who reasons from general logic about rain and roofs is demonstrating the same understanding.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe the features of a mountain environment — its animals, vegetation, and human adaptations in dress and housing — by reading a picture and connecting it to written information.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: One reason connected to heavy rainfall — e.g., slanting roofs allow rain or snow to slide off quickly, preventing the roof from collapsing under weight.

One reason connected to the cold climate or local resources — e.g., wood is available in mountain forests and is a good insulator against the cold; OR steep slopes mean flat-roofed structures would be harder to build and maintain.

assessment_items.question_text: Landslides are common in mountain areas during the rainy season. Explain why landslides happen in mountains, and describe two things a community can do to help people who are affected.
look_for: Provides a reason why landslides happen — e.g., heavy rain loosens soil and rocks on steep slopes; the slope makes soil unstable when saturated with water.
Names one concrete community action to help affected people — e.g., providing shelter, sharing food, helping rebuild, carrying out rescue.
Names a second community action that is different from the first.
Shows awareness that landslides are a natural hazard specific to mountain terrain, not a universal or random event.
Response demonstrates reasoning, not just recall — the student connects the mountain feature (steep slopes) to the hazard (landslide) to the community response.
assessment_items.annotation: This ECR assesses reasoning about hazard, terrain, and community resilience. Award full marks for a response that explains the mechanism of landslides and gives two distinct community actions. Spelling and grammar are not assessed.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain why a natural hazard occurs in a specific landform and identify safety and community response measures, using reasoning grounded in the features of that environment.

competency.competency_text: Discusses how to prepare for emergency situations (smoke, fire, small injuries, burns, electrical safety, unseasonal rains, fallen trees) based on discussions with family and community, or personal experiences

look_for: Provides a reason why landslides happen — e.g., heavy rain loosens soil and rocks on steep slopes; the slope makes soil unstable when saturated with water.
Names one concrete community action to help affected people — e.g., providing shelter, sharing food, helping rebuild, carrying out rescue.
Names a second community action that is different from the first.
Shows awareness that landslides are a natural hazard specific to mountain terrain, not a universal or random event.
Response demonstrates reasoning, not just recall — the student connects the mountain feature (steep slopes) to the hazard (landslide) to the community response.

assessment_items.task: Draw the landform of your own region in the space below. Label at least five things in your drawing: the type of landform, a typical plant, a typical animal, a type of house, and a food eaten by people there.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Landform type: ___
Plant: ___
Animal: ___
Type of house: ___
Food: ___
format_of_output: An annotated drawing of the student's local landform
Five labels: landform type, plant, animal, housing style, local food
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any regional landform and any locally accurate labels. The five labels are the assessment element — evaluate whether each one is genuinely connected to the student's local environment. Regional variation is expected and all accurate local answers are correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent their own geographical environment through annotated drawing, labelling the natural features and human practices that characterise it.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can accurately represent their own environment and connect its natural features to human life through annotated drawing.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold separates the five labels so the teacher can evaluate each element individually. A drawing with no labels scores zero on the five categories regardless of artistic quality.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: all five labels present, each accurate for the student's region, and the drawing clearly shows a recognisable landform. Weak: fewer than three labels, or labels that belong to a different region from the one the student described.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with drawing may describe their landform in a list instead; students who struggle to write labels may point to elements and have the teacher write them.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing is the mode prescribed in the textbook task for this section; it gives students who express better visually an equal opportunity to demonstrate geographical knowledge.

assessment_items.question_text: A student is filling the chapter's comparative table. In the 'Food' row, which entry correctly matches the desert column?

options.label: C
options.text: Makki di roti and sarson da saag

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is C. Dal-bati-churma and ker sangri are the foods described in the Rajasthan desert section. The other options are foods from the mountains (A), the coast (B), and the plains (D).
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can systematically compare features of different environments across multiple categories by completing a structured table that draws on details observed and discussed across a chapter.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

what_each_option_reveals.D: Places mountain foods (thukpa, sel roti) in the desert column — the student may have remembered these foods but not matched them to the correct landform.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Places coastal foods (dalma, pakhala) in the desert column — the student may be confusing the Odisha and Rajasthan sections.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Places plains foods (makki di roti, sarson da saag) in the desert column — the student may have remembered the first regional food taught and generalised it to all landforms.

assessment_items.task: Design an imaginary landform by combining two features from any two of the chapter's four landforms — plains, desert, coastal, or mountains. Draw it and write: (1) what two features you chose and where they come from, (2) one benefit this landform would give to people or animals, and (3) one difficulty people might face living there.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Feature 1: ___ (from the ___ landform)
Feature 2: ___ (from the ___ landform)
One benefit: ___
One difficulty: ___
format_of_output: A drawing of the imaginary composite landform
Written responses to all four scaffold prompts
assessment_items.annotation: Evaluate the reasoning in the written responses, not the drawing quality. A strong response names features that genuinely come from the chapter's four landforms, gives a plausible benefit, and names a real difficulty that follows logically from the chosen features.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design and justify a creative synthesis by selecting features from different environments, explaining the benefits each feature provides and the challenges it poses.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can transfer geographical knowledge into a creative reasoning task — selecting, combining, and evaluating landform features rather than simply recalling them.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Features 1 and 2 with their sources show whether the student accurately remembers which features belong to which landform. The benefit and difficulty prompts assess reasoning quality.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: both features correctly sourced to real chapter landforms, benefit is specific and logical, difficulty follows from the feature choice (e.g., choosing a desert feature means water shortage is a realistic difficulty). Weak: features not connected to any of the four landforms, or benefit and difficulty are identical or contradictory.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle to write may draw two panels showing the benefit and difficulty; students who find design difficult may describe their imaginary landform verbally to the teacher.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Annotated drawing with four written scaffold responses
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The draw-then-justify format matches the textbook's Let us reflect task and gives students a visual anchor before moving to the evaluative writing, reducing cognitive load while still requiring reasoned justification.
